D010-D006_h001.question:
I’ve been struggling for months—really, it started about seven months ago. At first, I was on fire: running the restaurant 18 hours a day, barely sleeping, talking so fast my staff couldn’t keep up. I was giddy one second, furious the next—over nothing, really. I spent thousands renovating a second location we can’t afford, and I was flirting with everyone, even customers, like I wasn’t married. Around that time, I started seeing figures in the kitchen when no one was there—shadowy people moving behind the line. And I became convinced my husband was cheating, even though he’s never given me a reason.  

Then, like a switch, it all crashed. For the last five months, I can’t get out of bed. I don’t care about the restaurant, don’t feel joy in anything, not even seeing my kids. I can’t decide what to wear, what to eat—simple things feel impossible. But here’s the thing: even when the crushing sadness came, those visions didn’t go away. And for two weeks last month, my mood was stable—no high, no low—but I still saw shadows and was certain my husband had installed hidden cameras in the house. The voices in my head, the jealousy, the visions—they were still here, even when the mania wasn’t.

D010-D006_h002.question:

During that time, I *knew* something was wrong inside me—felt like my stomach was rotting, even though doctors said I was fine. I kept tasting blood, nothing in my mouth, just blood. That didn’t stop when the manic phase faded. Even after the energy crashed and I fell into this deep hole—stopped talking, couldn’t focus, barely left bed for *five months*—those tastes and the belief that my body was decaying? They stayed. For over two weeks when I wasn’t manic *or* depressed, I still tasted metal and was sure my organs were failing. That’s when I knew it wasn’t just mood—it was something else, something separate, still clinging on.
D010-D006_h002.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    D. Adjustment Disorder

I felt unstoppable, like I was meant for something huge. During that time, I became totally convinced that this dispatcher at work, a woman I barely know, was secretly in love with me. I kept hearing her voice in my head, whispering things like, *“I’m always watching you,”* even when she wasn’t around.

But after that high faded, I crashed hard. For the last two months, I’ve barely been able to get out of bed. Moving feels heavy, like I’m underwater. I don’t care about work anymore, and my boss has warned me about missing calls. The same voices are still there—still talking to me, still saying she loves me—even when I’m not feeling manic. That’s the thing: they don’t go away, even when I’m low. I keep thinking, *I don’t want to be here anymore*. I don’t plan it, but the thought won’t leave. The psychosis is always present—before, during, and after the highs. The mania’s been there most of the time, but the voices and the delusion stick around when the mania’s gone—way more than two weeks now.

It started with this high energy—like I didn’t need sleep, I was calling clients at 3 a.m., tailing people all night, jumping from one case to another without finishing a single one. One minute I’d feel on top of the world, like I could crack any case, then suddenly I’d be furious at some imagined slight from a client or think my phone was tapped. I kept hearing whispers too—clear as day—like two guys in suits talking about me in low voices, even when no one was around. I started believing there was a conspiracy, maybe linked to a case I’d worked last year. I truly thought I was being followed, watched through cameras.

That manic phase lasted about two weeks, but even after it faded—the racing thoughts slowed a bit—I still heard those voices. They never really went away, even when I crashed into this deep funk where I couldn’t care less about cases, couldn’t get off the couch. I’d pace for hours, wringing my hands, and this urge would hit me—suddenly wanting to jump off my apartment roof, not because I wanted to die, but like the urge was just *there*, screaming.

The paranoia and voices stuck around for weeks after the mania was gone—still here some days.

I’ve been struggling for months now—this all started about two years ago, but the worst was two months ago when I couldn’t get out of bed. I felt completely numb, like my body was made of stone—moving, speaking, even lifting a cup took so much effort. I stopped caring about my writing, which used to be everything to me. I’d think, “What’s the point? None of it matters.” I even hoped I wouldn’t wake up some mornings, though I’d never act on it.

Before that, though, I was completely opposite—full of energy, up for days writing ten different stories, calling publishers at 3 a.m., starting book projects I never finished. I’d jump from one idea to another, convinced each was genius. I believed people on the radio were sending me coded messages about my work—specific compliments meant only I could understand. And sometimes, I’d taste something metallic in my mouth, even if I hadn’t eaten. My wife says it wasn’t real, but I *felt* it.

The key thing is, even when I wasn’t manic or depressed, those voices and tastes stuck around for weeks. And if I’m honest, the manic bursts have taken up most of the last two years.
